body.text: Donald Trump greets Xi Jinping on tarmac as three-day state visit begins
In short:
The US has rolled out the red carpet for China's President Xi Jinping, who has arrived in Washington for a three-day state visit.
Mr Trump personally greeted Mr Xi on arrival in a rare show of courtesy to his Chinese counterpart.
What's next?
AI, trade, Iran and Taiwan are all likely to be discussed in talks between the two leaders.

US President Donald Trump has greeted Chinese President Xi Jinping on the tarmac after arriving in the US, kicking off a three-day state visit aimed at smoothing simmering tensions between the superpowers.
However, the moment was not broadcast live on many US TV outlets, amid an ongoing protest over Mr Trump banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House.

Mr Trump and first lady Melania Trump shook hands with Mr Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, after the Chinese leader descended from his plane at Joint Base Andrews, a US military airfield outside Washington.
The two presidents stood side by side as a military band played, before two B-1 bombers staged a noisy flyover.

The personal airport greeting, a courtesy Mr Trump was notably denied when he visited Beijing in May, begins three days of pageantry that will include another flyover and a state banquet at the White House on Thursday, local time.
Six F-22 fighter jets and six F-16s were lined up on the tarmac in an apparent display of military might as US officials literally rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese leader.
Expectations of any major breakthroughs were low, but US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that both sides agreed to extend a tariff trade truce to January 10, 2027.
It had been due to expire in November.
"China and the United States should be partners, not rivals," Mr Xi said in a written statement released by the Chinese embassy that made no reference to a trade deal.
Mr Xi was accompanied by his right-hand man Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, among others, according to Chinese state media.

But there were no Chinese CEOs in his delegation, two sources told AFP, even though top US tech bosses, including the leaders of major AI companies, are set to attend Thursday's White House state banquet.

Mr Xi's visit will wrap up on Friday morning, local time, when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.
American presidents very rarely travel to the airport to greet foreign leaders, although Mr Trump welcomed Russian President Vladimir Putin as he stepped off his plane in Alaska last year.

The last such welcomes at Andrews, apart from papal visits, are believed to be John F Kennedy's welcome for British prime minister Harold Macmillan in 1962, and Dwight D Eisenhower's for Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in 1959.
AI on agenda

When the two leaders sit down for their highly anticipated talks later today, they will confront a host of thorny issues, led by fears — boosted by warnings from tech CEOs — that artificial intelligence risks wiping out humanity.
But with China and the United States racing for AI supremacy, there are few who expect any deal to regulate the rapidly advancing technology.

Jonathan Czin of the Brookings Institution told AFP that expectations for any concrete results from the meeting were low. However, he added: "I think there will be some extension of the gentleman's agreement."

Some China watchers told the ABC this week they saw the meeting as an opportunity to stabilise relations, while others cautioned that the carefully choreographed encounter could amount to little more than political theatre.
Preliminary talks on Sunday between the US Treasury secretary and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng included a discussion about creating a communication channel for AI concerns.
The two men held further "substantive" talks on Wednesday to prepare for Mr Xi's visit, Mr Bessent said in a statement.
Limited coverage of major arrival
Mr Trump's five-star welcome for Mr Xi has drawn criticism from China hawks within his own party, especially amid reports that Beijing has supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.

"Our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator," said Republican senator Roger Wicker, the chairman of the powerful Senate Armed Services Committee.
The US president, however, has played down the need to bring up the allegations of Chinese help for Iran, saying both Beijing and Washington spy on each other.

For Mr Trump, the state visit is also a chance to focus on pageantry instead of problems at home, where the Iran war's effect on fuel prices has sent his approval rating plummeting to historic lows ahead of the midterm elections in November.
The summit is taking place amid an unprecedented dispute between the White House and the US news media, with the traditional television press pool suspending its coverage.
A press pool is a group of news organisations that combine their resources to gather and distribute notes, news, photos and video.
They are created when space at, or access to, an event is limited.
The dispute began last week when the White House barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from its grounds, with Mr Trump accusing the outlets of what he called "fake news".

The three organisations have sued the administration, arguing the ban violates their First Amendment rights. The White House has said access to the building is a privilege and not a constitutional right.
The White House TV pool normally consists of crews from ABC (US), CBS, NBC, Fox News, and CNN, with the networks rotating responsibility for filming and distributing footage.
Because events such as meetings in the Oval Office are too small to accommodate every journalist, the pool footage is shared with a broader range of broadcasters and news organisations.
After the ban, the other four White House TV pool networks have decided not to send a replacement crew, in solidarity with CNN.
For the summit, the ban means Mr Xi's visit is unfolding with less independent television documentation.
The White House can still release its own photographs and video, while print, radio, and other journalists continue to cover the events.
It's not yet known what the ban and associated protest will mean for coverage of the rest of Mr Xi's state visit.
A judge said on Wednesday, local time, that he would rule soon on whether or not to reinstate White House press credentials.
The arrival of Mr Xi was still covered by news agencies including Reuters and Associated Press.
ABC/wires
